title: His Ship Sank in 2 Minutes. He Survived 133 Days Alone on a Raft
description:
Case 009, the full case file. Poon Lim was born on Hainan island, China, in 1918. As a teenager he went to sea as a cabin boy on a British ship, was treated badly and quit; when the war left Britain short of seamen he signed on again, and in November 1942 he was second steward on the SS Benlomond, a British cargo steamer that left Cape Town on 10 November bound for Suriname, armed but slow and sailing alone. On 23 November the German submarine U-172 hit her with two torpedoes and she sank in about two minutes. Poon Lim went into the sea in a life jacket and, after about two hours holding on to wreckage, found an empty wooden life raft about eight feet square with a canvas awning. It carried water, biscuits, chocolate, sugar, flares and a flashlight. Men on a second raft waved to him, but the rafts drifted apart; he was the only one of more than 50 aboard who was ever found.

He rationed the stores, tied a rope from his wrist to the raft and counted the days with knots. When the food and then the water ran out, he bent the flashlight's spring into a fish hook, unpicked rope for line, used biscuit and then small fish as bait, worked a nail out of the deck for a stronger hook, cut a knife from a tin, dried fish on a line and caught rain in the awning and the canvas cover of his life jacket. He caught seabirds, and after a storm ruined his fish and water he hooked a small shark and beat it on the deck with the water jug. When the sea was calm he swam round the raft to keep his strength. A freighter passed close enough to hear him and did not stop: he believed it was because he was Chinese, while others have pointed out that U-boats were rumoured to use a man on a raft as bait. American patrol planes spotted him and one dropped a marker buoy, but a storm moved the raft.

On 5 April 1943, after 133 days, three Brazilian fishermen picked him up off the coast of Pará and landed him at Belém three days later. He had lost about 20 pounds and spent weeks in hospital. In New York that July he was told that King George VI had awarded him the British Empire Medal, and his shipping line gave him a gold watch; the Royal Navy is said to have put his methods into its survival manuals. The US Navy turned him down for flat feet. After the war a senator won him an exception to the full Chinese immigration quota, he became a US citizen in 1952, went back to sea, and died in Brooklyn in 1991, aged 72. Guinness World Records still lists his 133 days as the longest survival alone on a raft. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. The officials, nurses, sailors and bystanders are stand-ins, not likenesses of anyone, and every card that looks like a document is an illustration.

source_notes:
LONG-FORM RUN (14 Nov 2026). Pages opened and read in full by this run: Wikipedia (Poon Lim), Today I Found Out (Matt Blitz, 'The Man on the Raft', 2014), The Old Salt Blog (Rick Spilman, 2013), War History Online (Clare Fitzgerald, 2021) and The Vintage News (2016). Guinness World Records, uboat.net and Wikipedia's ship article could not be re-opened by this run (the fetch permission timed out); what the film takes from them was read by the Short's run and its notes follow below unchanged. The US Navy photo caption was again not readable first-hand. Wikipedia's raft details cite George Blake's The Ben Line (1956) and Ruthanne Lum McCunn's Sole Survivor; several of its sentences carry 'citation needed' tags, named below, and the popular pages largely repeat one another, so the strength of the added facts is uneven and the script hedges where only one page says a thing. Added facts and where each was found: born 1918 in Hainan (Wikipedia: 8 March 1918, Wenchang County; War History Online; Today I Found Out). Cabin boy at sixteen on a British ship (Today I Found Out, The Vintage News), badly treated and quit (War History Online: 'poorly treated', swore off ships; Today I Found Out: seasick, teased, quit about 1937-38). 'Then the war comes, and the ships need men' paraphrases War History Online (Britain short of seamen in 1941 and recruiting in China). Left Cape Town on 10 November 1942 (Today I Found Out, War History Online) for Suriname/Paramaribo (Wikipedia, Today I Found Out, The Vintage News; War History Online wrongly calls Paramaribo Brazilian), 'armed but slow', alone (all). Two torpedoes (Old Salt, War History Online, The Vintage News, Short's sources). How he left the ship differs: washed overboard at his boat station as a lifeboat was being lowered (Wikipedia) or jumped (Old Salt, The Vintage News); the script says 'goes over the side' and the reused Short shot shows a jump, which is one of the two versions. A poor swimmer (Wikipedia, Today I Found Out, War History Online). Held a plank (Wikipedia: 'a few planks', used one for buoyancy). Stores: water (10 gallons / 40 litres), biscuits or hardtack, chocolate, sugar, flares, a flashlight (the items every list shares; Wikipedia adds pemmican, evaporated milk, lime juice and smoke pots; the insert says the lists differ). 'No way to steer it': Wikipedia says he could not propel the raft. A second raft with four or five men who waved him over, the rafts drifting apart (Wikipedia); War History Online tells it differently (five crewmen taken aboard the U-boat for questioning, put back, then gone), so the film shows only men waving and the rafts separating. Crew: 54 (uboat.net, War History Online) or 53 (Wikipedia, The Vintage News); Today I Found Out says 56 died; the card says MORE THAN 50. Expected quick rescue and rationed (Today I Found Out). Rope from wrist to raft (Wikipedia, War History Online, The Vintage News, Today I Found Out). Knots to count days, later full moons (Wikipedia, tagged citation needed; The Vintage News). Food about 55 days and water fifteen days more (Wikipedia; the US Navy caption per the Short's notes) against 'rationed for 30 days' (Today I Found Out): the script says 'about eight weeks' and 'about ten' and the insert says accounts differ. Hook from the flashlight spring (Wikipedia; 'wire' in the popular pages), line from unpicked hemp rope, hardtack as bait, small fish as bait for bigger ones, a nail dug from the boards for a stronger hook, knife from a tin (pemmican tin in Wikipedia, biscuit tin elsewhere; 'a tin'), fish dried on a line (Wikipedia, The Vintage News, War History Online). Rain in the awning and the canvas life-jacket cover (Wikipedia, The Vintage News, Today I Found Out). The seaweed nest baited with fish is in Today I Found Out only, so the narration says 'by one account' and the shot carries that label; Wikipedia says only that gulls which settled on the raft were killed. The storm that spoiled his fish and fouled his water (The Vintage News; Today I Found Out has a storm in the second month that cost him his water and food). The shark: line braided double, hands wrapped in canvas, bird remains as bait, hauled aboard, fought on deck, beaten with the water container (Wikipedia, The Vintage News; Today I Found Out agrees in outline); 'a small one' follows The Vintage News ('only a few feet long'); the narration says the shark was 'his water as well as his food' in place of the reported detail that he drank blood from its liver (Wikipedia, The Vintage News), which is not shown; fins dried in the sun, a Hainan delicacy (Wikipedia, tagged citation needed; The Vintage News; Today I Found Out). Swimming round the raft twice a day in calm weather (Old Salt, Today I Found Out), not with sharks about (The Vintage News). The freighter: seen and not picked up despite his shouts in English (Wikipedia); his own belief that it was because he was Chinese (Today I Found Out, The Vintage News; Wikipedia: that they took him for a Japanese sailor); the other explanation, that U-boats were rumoured to set a 'survivor' on a raft as a trap (Wikipedia, War History Online, The Vintage News, all as a rumour or general claim). The film gives both, attributes each, and does not choose; Rook makes no joke in that segment. Wikipedia speaks of several cargo ships; the film shows one. Patrol planes, a marker buoy, and a storm that moved the raft (Wikipedia, tagged citation needed; War History Online; Today I Found Out without the buoy). Sea no longer deep-ocean blue by April 1943, and a drift of about 750 miles (Wikipedia). 5 April 1943, three Brazilian fishermen (Guinness and uboat.net per the Short's notes, Wikipedia, Old Salt; 'a fishing family' in Today I Found Out), waving a shirt and jumping (Today I Found Out). Three days to Belem (Wikipedia, Today I Found Out). About 20 lb / 9 kg lost (all). Hospital: four weeks (Today I Found Out, War History Online, The Vintage News), two weeks or 45 days (both in Wikipedia): 'weeks'. New York, 16 July 1943, where the acting British consul told him of the award of the British Empire Medal by King George VI, and the Ben Line gave him a gold watch (Wikipedia; the popular pages say the King presented it in Britain, which Wikipedia's dated account does not support, so the narration says 'awards him' and the shot shows an unnamed official, not the King). Royal Navy survival manuals (Wikipedia, tagged citation needed; Today I Found Out, War History Online, The Vintage News): the insert is marked as an illustration. Turned down by the US Navy for flat feet (Wikipedia only); the narration places it before the post-war sentences but Wikipedia gives no date for it. Quota full, special dispensation with the help of Senator Warren Magnuson, citizen in 1952 (Wikipedia, The Vintage News, War History Online); the senator is not named or shown. Back to sea with United States Lines, retiring as chief steward in 1983 (Wikipedia; the script says only that he went back to sea). Died in Brooklyn on 4 January 1991 aged 72 (Wikipedia, War History Online; Old Salt says 73). The remark about the record is given as reported speech ('he is reported to have said he hoped nobody would ever have to break that record') because its wording differs between pages; it is not shown as a quotation on screen. 'Nobody has' rests on Guinness (per the Short's run), Wikipedia and Old Salt, and means alone on a raft: longer drifts in boats are a different record. Left out because this run could not stand them up or they did not fit: that the U-boat's crew laughed and waved him away (Wikipedia); a later U-boat that surfaced near the raft (Today I Found Out, War History Online, The Vintage News; cut for length); the Ministry of Information film; his marriage and children; the wartime treatment of Chinese seamen generally (true and documented, but a subject of its own); that he walked ashore unaided (sources conflict). Dramatised, not reported, in addition to the Short's list: the mess room and everything in it, the officers at the table and the mop (that he was a cabin boy and was badly treated is sourced; the scene is invented staging and nobody in it is a likeness); the Cape Town quay, crane, sheds and bystanders and the mountain behind (a flat-topped mountain stands behind that harbour; the rest is set dressing); Rook in the water on a plank; the look and number of the men on the second raft (three figures stand in for 'four or five'); the biscuit broken in half; Rook's ankle rope; the hands tying knots; the size of the bigger fish; Rook sniffing the dried fish; the shape of the seaweed nest; the tins knocked over after the storm; how the shark fight looked (no blood is shown); Rook up the awning pole; the freighter's look and the three figures at its rail; the marker buoy's shape, colour and dye and Rook sitting on it (a visual way to say the marker stayed and the raft did not; the narration says so in words); the gulls; the green of the water; the Belem waterfront, its houses, church and palms, and the people waiting; the ward, the nurse and the bowl; the hall in New York, its drapes, stage and audience, and the official; the hands passing the watch; the recruiting desk, the height chart and the man behind the desk; the stoop in Brooklyn, the old man sitting on it and the empty step in the last scene; every card, form, certificate, manual page, scale and bar chart (each is labelled an illustration or a sketch); and everything Rook does. No dialogue is attributed to anyone.

SHORT'S NOTES (r009-poonlim): Read for this run (fetched 14 Nov 2026): Guinness World Records ('Longest time adrift at sea - alone'), uboat.net (ship page for Benlomond), Wikipedia (Poon Lim; SS Benlomond (1922)), War History Online and Today I Found Out. The strong sources are Guinness, uboat.net and the US Navy caption to photo 80-G-42356 (July 1943, read second-hand via Wikipedia); the popular articles largely repeat Wikipedia, which cites the New York Times of 17 July 1943 and London Gazette 36091, neither of which this run could open. Agreed: SS Benlomond of the Ben Line, unescorted, between Cape Town and Paramaribo; sunk 23 November 1942 by U-172 with two torpedoes; sank in about two minutes (uboat.net, both Wikipedia pages); Poon Lim was the second (mess) steward and the only survivor (Guinness, uboat.net, Wikipedia); born in Hainan in March 1918, so 24 at the sinking (Wikipedia, the popular articles; the US Navy caption calls him 25 in July 1943, which fits); about two hours in the water before he found the raft; a wooden raft about eight feet square with biscuits/hardtack, water and other stores, flares and a flashlight; a fish hook made from the flashlight's spring (US Navy caption and every other source), a larger hook from a nail, hemp rope as line, rain caught in canvas, seabirds and a shark caught; a passing freighter that did not pick him up and US Navy patrol planes that saw him before a storm moved him; rescue on 5 April 1943 by three Brazilian fishermen about ten miles off the coast of Para, landed at Belem three days later; about 20 lb / 9 kg lost; British Empire Medal; US citizenship in 1952; died in Brooklyn on 4 January 1991; Guinness: 'the longest recorded survival alone on a raft is 133 days', still listed. Where the sources differ: (1) Men aboard: 54 with 53 lost (uboat.net) or 53 with 52 lost (Wikipedia); the description says 'more than 50' and the film gives no number. (2) Position: 0.5 N 38.75 W (uboat.net, ship article) or 0.3 N 38.45 W (Poon Lim article); the sketch map uses the first and is labelled a sketch. (3) Birthplace: Hainan (Wikipedia and others) or 'Hong Kong-born' (Guinness); the crew-file insert says Hainan, China. (4) How long the stores lasted: food about 55 days and water about 70 (Wikipedia, US Navy caption) or rationed for 30 days (Today I Found Out); the script says only 'Then nothing' and gives no figure. (5) The knife: cut from a biscuit tin (War History Online) or a pemmican tin (Wikipedia); the script says 'a tin'. (6) Rescue date 5 April (Guinness, uboat.net, Wikipedia) or 4 April (US Navy caption); the map says 5 April. (7) Some sources count 132 days; Guinness says 133. (8) Whether he walked ashore unaided (Guinness) or had to be lifted off the raft (Wikipedia); not shown or stated. (9) Hospital stay of four weeks or two; not stated. (10) Other men were seen on a second raft that drifted away and was never found (Wikipedia), and uboat.net says the U-boat's crew questioned survivors; nobody else was ever rescued, the film does not show this. Left out on purpose: his belief that the freighter did not stop because he was Chinese / might be taken for Japanese (reported as his view by Wikipedia and others; a Short has no room to present it fairly, so the film says only that the ship did not stop; the label reads IT KEEPS GOING); drinking the shark's blood; the quote often attributed to him about hoping nobody breaks the record (wording varies and no primary source was found, so it is not used). No dialogue is attributed to anyone. Shown but not narrated, from the sources: the life jacket, the U-boat and the torpedo track, the knotted rope for counting days (Wikipedia, The Vintage News), fish strips drying on a line (Wikipedia), the canvas awning (Wikipedia, Today I Found Out), 23 NOV 1942 and 5 APR 1943 on the map. Dramatised, not reported: the look of the ship (a generic grey 1920s steamer with no name, flag or company colours), of the submarine (no number or emblem), of the passing freighter and the patrol plane (generic twin-engined flying boat, no markings); the raft's floats, poles and exact layout, the tins' colours and the water can; how he looked and dressed; the gull landing on Rook's hat and the way the bird is caught; the shark circling at the surface (sources say he hooked a small shark, not how it approached); the storm's lightning; the fishermen's boat, sail, hats and clothes and their number in the last shot; the hand clasp; the coastline; the crew-file card (a drawn silhouette, not a photograph; no such document is claimed); the dotted drift line (its real path is unknown and the map says so); the harbour pier; and everything Rook does. Rook is never the one in danger in the sad beats: he drops the jokes when the freighter passes.
